rv.q: It’s thought-provoking, but too heavily signposted to truly hit you in the heart.
This is as close to perfect theatre as you can get.
Daniel’s Husband offers 90 minutes of quality, thought-provoking theatre, and McKeever reaffirms his growing reputation as a writer of significance.

It’s typical of a few segments where characters are required by the script to express opinions which feel unnecessary and forced, simply as a means of tidying historical loose ends and generating theatrical friction.
A modern fable about the dangers of procrastination, there’s much food for thought in this intense and compelling production.
However, in its attempts to make not wanting to get married into a kind of tragic flaw, Daniel’s Husband has wound up contradicting and simplifying its own messages.
This is a profoundly affecting piece of contemporary theatre, rich in emotional depth and moral complexity and could sit shoulder to shoulder with any classic in the West End.
Despite those final steps in the right direction, Daniel’s Husband‘s real potential remains in the shadows for the most part.

cn.t: McKeever's drama about marriage and power of attorney in a gay relationship provokes thought with its timely themes, though critics find it overly signposted. Praise centers on the set design and performances in this mixed reception UK premiere.
